meta.title: Who really said "How old would you be if you didn't know how old you was"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Satchel Paige, but the saying was preached in Brooklyn in 1927. Paige's name only attached in 1977. The documented chronology, sourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'How old would you be if you didn't know how old you was?'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Satchel Paige, on the evidence. The question appears in a 1927 Brooklyn sermon; Paige's name was attached to it fifty years later.

answer.label: Not Satchel Paige’s line — it was in print by 1927
answer.authorDates: Congregational minister, Brooklyn · earliest documented use, 1927
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known appearance is a sermon by Rev. Clarence H. Wilson at the Flatbush Congregational Church in Brooklyn, reported in The Brooklyn Daily Eagle on 24 October 1927 — roughly two decades before Satchel Paige reached the major leagues. The earliest located attribution to Paige is 1977, and no primary source in which Paige himself says it has been located. Quote Investigator calls Wilson the originator only tentatively ↗, so treat the credit as earliest-documented, not settled.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed: an earlier documented source exists, and no Paige primary source does.

source.excerpt: How old would you be if you didn’t know how old you are?
trail: 1927 — Brooklyn. Rev. Clarence H. Wilson asks the question in a sermon at the Flatbush Congregational Church; The Brooklyn Daily Eagle prints it on 24 October. This is the earliest match Quote Investigator has located ↗.

1931–1962 — the saying travels ownerless. Wallace R. Farrington uses it at a University of Maine commencement in 1931; Howard Thornton poses it at an Oklahoma Kiwanis Club in 1960; G. Herbert True reorders it in 1962 — none of them crediting Paige ↗.
1977–78 — the name lands. Ruth Gordon credits Paige in House testimony; Garson Kanin prints the “how old you was” wording under Paige’s name in 1978. Both are secondhand recollections ↗.
Today — still unsourced to Paige. The line appears in Wikiquote’s “Unsourced” list for Paige ↗, while his genuinely cited age material — the 1953 Collier’s rules — sits in the sourced section.
source.excerptNote: This is the 1927 wording as reported from Wilson’s sermon. The familiar dialect form — “how old you was” — is not documented until 1978, in Garson Kanin’s It Takes a Long Time To Become Young, where it already carries Paige’s name.
source.rightsNote: Rights here are genuinely unclear, so we assert nothing. The 1927 Brooklyn Daily Eagle report of Wilson’s sermon predates 1931 and that specific published text would be out of copyright — but the wording quoted today, with “how old you was,” is first documented in a 1978 book that remains in copyright. Since we cannot tie the popular wording to any pre-1931 printing, we decline to call it public domain.

author.name: Rev. Clarence H. Wilson
author.heading: The Brooklyn preacher who got there first
author.metaLine: Congregational minister, Flatbush, Brooklyn · earliest documented use, 1927
author.bio: Almost nothing is publicly recorded about Rev. Clarence H. Wilson beyond the pulpit he occupied: the Flatbush Congregational Church in Brooklyn, where he preached a sermon reported by The Brooklyn Daily Eagle on 24 October 1927. One line from it — “How old would you be if you didn’t know how old you are?” — is the oldest known instance of a question that would circulate, unattributed, for the next fifty years. Quote Investigator names him the originator only provisionally; he is best understood as the earliest voice we can currently document, not a proven author.

misattribution.heading: How the credit drifted
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook orphan aphorism: it circulated for half a century with no fixed owner, then attached itself to the most famous man in America with a disputed birthday.

items.why: Paige’s name enters the record in 1977, when actress Ruth Gordon credited him during U.S. House testimony, and again in 1978 when her husband Garson Kanin printed it in It Takes a Long Time To Become Young. Both are secondhand. Wikiquote keeps the line in its “Unsourced” section ↗.

The dialect form that dominates today is not the older wording. No documented instance before 1977 uses the “was” form — the earlier citations read “how old you are” or “how old you were” — and “was” is first documented in Kanin’s 1978 book ↗, already under Paige’s name.
Dyer printed the expression in The Sky’s the Limit in 1980 without attribution ↗, which helped it spread through self-help writing as an unowned maxim.

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest known instance belongs to a Brooklyn preacher, not a pitcher: Rev. Clarence H. Wilson, in a sermon reported by The Brooklyn Daily Eagle on 24 October 1927 — though Quote Investigator holds even that attribution open ↗ pending an earlier citation.

context.heading: Why the line stuck to Satchel Paige
lead: Of all the famous names this aphorism could have landed on, Paige was the most magnetic. His age was the great open question of American baseball: reported birth years ranged across roughly a decade, and his actual date — 7 July 1906 — was only pinned down in 1948, when Cleveland owner Bill Veeck went to Mobile, Alabama and had the birth certificate pulled. Paige then debuted in the majors at 42 and was still pitching three shutout innings at 59.

So a floating question about not knowing your own age fit him like a glove — and the dialect wording that circulates today, with “how old you was,” is part of the fit. That phrasing first shows up in print in 1978, in Garson Kanin’s It Takes a Long Time To Become Young, where it is set under Paige’s name. It reads like Paige. That is not the same as being documented from Paige.
context.detailsSummary: What Paige is actually on the record for
detailsBody: Paige has plenty of genuinely sourced material on aging — most famously the “How to Stay Young” rules published in Collier’s on 13 June 1953, which Wikiquote lists with a full citation ↗. The “how old would you be” question is not among them; it sits in the unsourced pile instead.

The saying travelled widely on its own before Paige’s name arrived. Quote Investigator records Wallace R. Farrington using it at a University of Maine commencement in 1931, Howard Thornton posing it at an Oklahoma Kiwanis Club in 1960, a reordered version from G. Herbert True in 1962, and Wayne W. Dyer printing it with no attribution at all in 1980.
context.pull: A question with no owner found a man with no birthday.
